summary.text: Writing \(p=2m+1\), Lucas congruences split the defining sums at \(p\) and pair the terms indexed by \(k\) and \(p+k\), giving vanishing at every \(p+r\) with \(0\le r<p-1\); moreover \(\binom{p-1}{k}\equiv(-1)^k\) gives the first anti-diagonal value \(1\), while central-binomial vanishing leaves only \(k=m\) in the second, giving \((-1)^m\). Thus both Hankel matrices are anti-triangular modulo \(p\), and multiplying their anti-diagonal entries by the reversal sign \((-1)^{p(p-1)/2}=(-1)^{pm}\) yields the two stated residues.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^4
\]
and
\[
c(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^2\binom{2k}{k}
                 \binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}.
\]
Fix an odd prime \(p\), and write
\[
p=2m+1,\qquad m=\frac{p-1}{2}.
\]
All congruences below are modulo \(p\).

We first establish the binomial congruences that will be used to simplify the two Hankel matrices.

### 1. Binomial congruences modulo \(p\)

We use the following one-step form of Lucas' congruence. If
\[
n=qp+r,\qquad k=sp+t,\qquad 0\le r,t<p,
\]
then
\[
\binom nk\equiv \binom qs\binom rt\pmod p.
\tag{1}
\]
For completeness, this follows from the polynomial identity over \(\mathbb F_p\)
\[
(1+x)^p=1+x^p.
\]
Indeed,
\[
(1+x)^n=(1+x)^{qp+r}=(1+x^p)^q(1+x)^r.
\]
The coefficient of \(x^{sp+t}\) on the right is \(\binom qs\binom rt\), with the convention that \(\binom rt=0\) when \(t>r\), proving (1).

For \(0\le k<p\), we have
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}\equiv(-1)^k.
\tag{2}
\]
One way to see this directly is to begin with \(\binom{p-1}{0}=1\) and use
\[
(k+1)\binom{p-1}{k+1}=(p-1-k)\binom{p-1}{k}.
\]
Modulo \(p\), the right side is \(-(k+1)\binom{p-1}{k}\). Since \(k+1\not\equiv0\pmod p\) for \(k+1<p\), cancellation gives the induction step
\(
\binom{p-1}{k+1}\equiv-\binom{p-1}{k}.
\)
The final case \(k=p-1\) also agrees with (2), or follows directly.

Now let \(0\le r<p\). Applying (1) gives, for \(0\le k<p\),
\[
\binom{p+r}{k}\equiv \binom rk.
\tag{3}
\]
In particular this is zero if \(r<k<p\). Likewise, for \(0\le j<p\),
\[
\binom{p+r}{p+j}\equiv\binom rj.
\tag{4}
\]

We shall also need a congruence involving central binomial coefficients:
\[
\binom{2p+2u}{p+u}\equiv 2\binom{2u}{u}
\qquad(0\le u<p).
\tag{5}
\]
There are two cases.

If \(2u<p\), then the base-\(p\) decompositions are
\[
2p+2u=2p+(2u),\qquad p+u=p+u.
\]
Thus (1) gives
\[
\binom{2p+2u}{p+u}
 \equiv \binom21\binom{2u}{u}
 =2\binom{2u}{u}.
\]

If \(p\le 2u<2p\), then \((2u)\bmod p=2u-p<u\). Applying (1) to \(\binom{2u}{u}\), whose lower argument has low base-\(p\) digit \(u\), shows
\[
\binom{2u}{u}\equiv0.
\]
For the left side of (5), the low digit of \(2p+2u\) is again \(2u-p\), while the low digit of \(p+u\) is \(u\). Since \(2u-p<u\), its Lucas factor is also zero. Thus both sides of (5) vanish in this case, proving (5) in all cases.

A related consequence will be useful later. If \(p=2m+1\) and
\[
m<k<p,
\]
then
\[
\binom{2k}{k}\equiv0.
\tag{6}
\]
Indeed, \(p\le2k<2p\), so the low base-\(p\) digit of \(2k\) is \(2k-p\). Since \(k<p\), the low digit of the lower argument is \(k\), and
\(
2k-p<k.
\)
Lucas' congruence therefore gives zero.

### 2. The values of \(a(n)\) needed for the determinant

First consider \(a(p-1)\). By (2),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(p-1)
&=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\binom{p-1}{k}^4\\
&\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\bigl((-1)^k\bigr)^4\\
&=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k.
\end{aligned}
\]
There are an odd number \(p=2m+1\) of summands. The first \(2m\) terms cancel in adjacent pairs \(1-1\), and the last term is \(1\). Hence
\[
a(p-1)\equiv1.
\tag{7}
\]

Next, for every integer \(r\) satisfying
\[
0\le r<p-1,
\]
we claim
\[
a(p+r)\equiv0.
\tag{8}
\]
Split the defining sum for \(a(p+r)\) into the three ranges
\[
0\le k\le r,\qquad r<k<p,\qquad k=p+j\ (0\le j\le r).
\]
In the middle range, (3) gives \(\binom{p+r}{k}\equiv0\), so every term vanishes.

In the first range, (3) gives
\[
(-1)^k\binom{p+r}{k}^4
 \equiv(-1)^k\binom rk^4.
\]
In the last range, (4) and the oddness of \(p\) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
(-1)^{p+j}\binom{p+r}{p+j}^4
&\equiv-(-1)^j\binom rj^4.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the term indexed by \(j\) in the last range is the negative of the term indexed by \(j\) in the first range. The two ranges cancel term by term, proving (8).

### 3. The values of \(c(n)\) needed for the determinant

We first prove that, just as for \(a\),
\[
c(p+r)\equiv0\qquad(0\le r<p-1).
\tag{9}
\]
Again divide the sum into
\[
0\le k\le r,\qquad r<k<p,\qquad k=p+j\ (0\le j\le r).
\]
The middle range vanishes because \(\binom{p+r}{k}\equiv0\) there.

For \(0\le k\le r\), put \(u=r-k\). Then
\[
p+r-k=p+u.
\]
Using (3) and (5), the corresponding summand satisfies
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(-1)^k\binom{p+r}{k}^2\binom{2k}{k}
                 \binom{2(p+r-k)}{p+r-k}\\
&\quad\equiv
(-1)^k\binom rk^2\binom{2k}{k}
                 \left(2\binom{2(r-k)}{r-k}\right).
\tag{10}
\end{aligned}
\]

For a term in the last range, write \(k=p+j\), where \(0\le j\le r\). Then
\[
p+r-(p+j)=r-j.
\]
By (4), (5), and \((-1)^{p+j}=-(-1)^j\), this summand is congruent to
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(-1)^{p+j}\binom{p+r}{p+j}^2
 \binom{2(p+j)}{p+j}\binom{2(r-j)}{r-j}\\
&\quad\equiv
-(-1)^j\binom rj^2
 \left(2\binom{2j}{j}\right)\binom{2(r-j)}{r-j}.
\tag{11}
\end{aligned}
\]
The expression in (11) is exactly the negative of (10) with \(k=j\). Hence the first and last ranges cancel term by term, proving (9).

It remains to determine \(c(p-1)\). Since \(p-1=2m\), its defining sum is
\[
c(p-1)=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\binom{p-1}{k}^2
       \binom{2k}{k}\binom{2(p-1-k)}{p-1-k}.
\]
We show that all terms except \(k=m\) vanish modulo \(p\).

If \(k>m\), then \(k<p\), and (6) gives
\(
\binom{2k}{k}\equiv0.
\)
If \(k<m\), set
\[
\ell=p-1-k=2m-k.
\]
Then \(m<\ell<p\), so (6), now applied to \(\ell\), gives
\[
\binom{2(p-1-k)}{p-1-k}=\binom{2\ell}{\ell}\equiv0.
\]
Thus only \(k=m\) survives.

At \(k=m\), we have \(p-1-m=m\) and \(2m=p-1\). By (2),
\[
\binom{p-1}{m}\equiv(-1)^m,
\qquad
\binom{2m}{m}=\binom{p-1}{m}\equiv(-1)^m.
\]
Both central-binomial factors in the summand are the same. Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
c(p-1)
&\equiv (-1)^m\bigl((-1)^m\bigr)^2
                 (-1)^m(-1)^m\\
&=(-1)^{5m}=(-1)^m.
\end{aligned}
\tag{12}
\]
Here the last equality follows because \((-1)^{4m}=1\).

### 4. An anti-triangular determinant lemma

Let \(R\) be a commutative ring, and let \(M=(M_{ij})_{0\le i,j<p}\) be a \(p\times p\) matrix such that
\[
M_{ij}=0\quad\text{whenever }i+j\ge p.
\tag{13}
\]
Let \(\rho\) be the reversal permutation
\[
\rho(i)=p-1-i.
\]
We claim
\[
\det M=\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)
       \prod_{i=0}^{p-1}M_{\rho(i),i}.
\tag{14}
\]

To prove this, consider a term associated with a permutation \(\sigma\) in the Leibniz expansion of the determinant. If this term can be nonzero, (13) requires
\[
\sigma(i)+i\le p-1
\qquad\text{for every }i.
\tag{15}
\]
On the other hand, because \(\sigma\) is a permutation,
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}(\sigma(i)+i)
=2\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}i
=p(p-1).
\tag{16}
\]
The sum of the \(p\) upper bounds in (15) is also \(p(p-1)\). Consequently equality must hold in every one of the inequalities (15):
\[
\sigma(i)+i=p-1\quad\text{for all }i.
\]
Thus \(\sigma(i)=p-1-i=\rho(i)\) for every \(i\). Every permutation other than \(\rho\) has at least one zero matrix factor, so the sole surviving Leibniz term is the one in (14).

The reversal permutation has sign
\[
\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)=(-1)^{p(p-1)/2}.
\tag{17}
\]
Indeed, every pair \(i<j\) is reversed by \(\rho\), so \(\rho\) has exactly \(\binom p2=p(p-1)/2\) inversions.

Equivalently, one can obtain (17) by considering the anti-identity matrix \(J\), with \(J_{ij}=1\) when \(i+j=p-1\) and \(0\) otherwise. Formula (14) gives \(\det J=\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)\). Expanding \(J\) along its first row leaves only the final entry, whose cofactor is the anti-identity matrix of size \(p-1\); induction yields \(\det J=(-1)^{p(p-1)/2}\).

### 5. The determinant formed from \(a(n)\)

Let
\[
A=(a(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}.
\]
Reduce all entries modulo \(p\), viewing \(A\) as a matrix over \(\mathbb F_p\). Determinants commute with reduction modulo \(p\), since a determinant is an integer polynomial in the entries.

If \(i+j\ge p\), then, because \(i,j\le p-1\), we may write
\[
i+j=p+r,
\qquad 0\le r\le p-2.
\]
By (8), \(a(i+j)=a(p+r)\equiv0\). Thus the reduced matrix satisfies the anti-triangular vanishing condition (13).

Every entry on the anti-diagonal has index sum \(p-1\), and by (7) it is congruent to \(1\). Applying (14) and (17),
\[
\det A\equiv(-1)^{p(p-1)/2}.
\]
Since \(p=2m+1\),
\[
\frac{p(p-1)}2=pm.
\]
The integer \(p\) is odd, so \((-1)^{pm}=(-1)^m\). As \(m=(p-1)/2\), this gives
\[
\boxed{\det(a(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}
\equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p.}
\]

### 6. The determinant formed from \(c(n)\)

Now let
\[
C=(c(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}.
\]
As above, if \(i+j\ge p\), then \(i+j=p+r\) for some \(0\le r\le p-2\), and (9) gives
\[
c(i+j)\equiv0.
\]
Thus the reduction of \(C\) modulo \(p\) is also anti-triangular.

By (12), every one of its \(p\) anti-diagonal entries is congruent to \((-1)^m\). Therefore (14) and (17) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\det C
&\equiv (-1)^{p(p-1)/2}\prod_{i=0}^{p-1}(-1)^m\\
&=(-1)^{pm}\bigl((-1)^m\bigr)^p\\
&=(-1)^{pm}(-1)^{mp}\\
&=(-1)^{2mp}=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{\det(c(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}\equiv1\pmod p.}
\]

Both asserted congruences therefore hold for every odd prime \(p\).
